newsitem.title: PERU: Siege explosion shakes Peru from Christmas lull.
newsitem.headline: Siege explosion shakes Peru from Christmas lull.

text.p: A loud explosion early on Thursday shattered a Christmas lull in tension at the Japanese embassy residence in Lima where Marxist rebels held 104 VIP hostages under the gun for a ninth day.
"The explosion came from within the residence at the back part. We are trying to investigate it but we cannot get very close," said Nestor Ramos, a police officer at the site.

Police added the explosion -- heard at around 1:45 A.M. local time (0645 GMT) -- came from inside the residence grounds behind the building that houses the captives, including government officials, Japanese businessmen and some foreign diplomats.

There were no immediate reports of injuries and television images showed no damage to the building. It was not clear who was responsible for the explosion nor if it was triggered deliberately or by accident.
Some of the released hostages have said they believe the rebels have put booby-traps and landmines around the residence in a bid to secure the building.
Thursday's explosion, which police estimated had a strength equal to no more than four sticks of dynamite, was followed by an eery silence from within the residence, witnesses said.
They said that prior to the explosion they saw no unusual movement by the 900-strong police force deployed at the site.
An unconfirmed television report said two men were seen running away from the residence compound over nearby roofs shortly after the explosion.

To add to the uncertainty, a Red Cross official ran from his nightwatch post through police lines after the explosion to call for the immediate presence of colleague Michel Minnig -- the chief negotiator in the crisis.
But as there were no further incidents, the Red Cross said Minnig would go to the residence only later on Thursday.

The explosion came hours after the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels freed on Wednesday one sick Japanese hostage and allowed the other 104 to enjoy a Catholic mass and a turkey Christmas lunch sent by President Alberto Fujimori.
The released man, Kenji Hirata, 34, his head slumped to one side, was pushed out of the residence in a wheelchair by Red Cross workers.

A police ambulance sped Hirata -- a first secretary at the Japanese embassy in Lima -- away to a nearby hospital, where he was placed on an intravenous drip and treated for dehydration. The Red Cross said his condition was stable but relatives in Japan said they were worried about his health.
Hirata's release was the first since Uruguayan Ambassador Tabare Bocalandro's liberation on Tuesday after his government freed two MRTA guerrillas from jail.
Furious at the apparent concession, Peru recalled its top diplomat from Uruguay. Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto also criticised the apparent swap.
"The Uruguay government has explained that there was no link between the two (release of the two rebels and the Lima hostage issue)," Hashimoto told reporters in Tokyo.
"I don't know whether this is true or not, but in any case it has made a solution of the case difficult," he said. "We must not surrender to terrorism."
Japan has about 30 nationals inside the besieged residence, including Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated cocktail reception that was stormed by the MRTA rebels.
Foreign Ministry officials said Japan's prime minister and foreign minister were both considering cancelling foreign trips in January because of the continuing hostage crisis.
Fujimori has flatly rejected all the demands made by the guerrillas and has said they must release the captives and hand over their weapons.

The rebels have vowed not to surrender until the government releases more than 400 MRTA members from Peruvian jails. They also want an end to free-market economic policies and more state support for the country's impoverished majority.

Japanese media covering the crisis speculated a behind-the-scenes deal might be worked out to allow the MRTA captors to fly to asylum in Cuba after releasing the hostages, but there has been no official word on this.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi arrived in Lima early on Thursday to try to secure the release of his country's ambassador to Peru, Ahmad Mokhtar.
The decision to send the foreign minister sparked rumours in Peru that Malaysia would try to cut a behind-the-scenes deal with the guerrillas holding its envoy.
